country.comment: Historical-institutional case study of Barcelona (and neighbouring municipalities on the Plain of Barcelona aggregated in 1897), Spain.
country.where_found: PDF p. 2, Title, affiliation, and Abstract; PDF p. 18, Conclusion

effect_estimate.comment: Historical-institutional study reporting descriptive archival figures rather than inferential statistical effect estimates (e.g., 1859 inspection found 90% of Barcelona streets had sewers, 57% in good condition, while 81% of streets in working-class La Barceloneta lacked sewers; private SGAB catchments rose from 15,000 m3 in 1890 to 81,000 m3 in 1910 and 150,000 m3/day [200,000 m3/day citywide, or 200 L/inhabitant/day] in 1929; per-capita consumption doubled between 1910 and 1943; SGAB imposed supply restrictions during 30% of service hours starting May 1953 before 1955–1967 surface-water transfers generalized domestic access).
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric statistical effect estimate reported. Archival analysis shows that municipal fiscal constraints, the omission of water and sewerage from the 1859 Eixample expansion plan, failed municipalization of the private monopoly Sociedad General de Aguas de Barcelona (SGAB), high connection and fixture costs, and tenement landlords' preference for building-wide trickle-feed contracts over individual meters (despite the 1925 Municipal Health Regulations) confined modern domestic water and sewered sanitation to affluent central areas while excluding working-class districts; widespread domestic access across social strata was achieved only after surface-water catchments from the Llobregat (1955–1965) and Ter River (1967) ended post-war supply restrictions (which reached 30% of service hours in May 1953).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 by the study design ceiling (Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework). Primary municipal and utility archival records directly document the operation of planning omissions, fee/concession barriers, private utility cherry-picking of affluent areas, failed municipalization, and landlord trickle-feed contracting versus statutory metering rules on household water and sanitation access.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines landlord-tenant tenement contracting and Crown/municipal vs. private monopoly ownership (tenure, property), the 1859 Eixample expansion plan and 1891/1902 sewerage plans/ordinances and building permits (planning, building_permit), municipal boundaries/1897 aggregation, elevation limits, and private network concentration in central affluent districts (service_area), ploma/connection fees and tariffs (fees), multi-decade municipal infrastructure and river-transfer delays (delay), pre-1791 merit-based discretionary water concessions (discretion), and municipal-utility-state fragmentation, failed municipalization, and coordination over Llobregat and Ter surface-water transfers (institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, tenure, property, planning, building_permit, service_area, fees, delay, discretion, institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination

outcome_flags.comment: Analyzes domestic piped water and continuous-circulation sewer connections (formal_connection, water_access, sanitation_access), unequal spatial network coverage across central affluent vs. peripheral working-class districts and La Barceloneta (service_coverage), per-capita water volumes and trickle-feed contract limits (service_quantity), well contamination from nearby cesspits and the 1914 Montcada typhoid epidemic (service_quality), high connection/appliance costs and tenant affordability constraints (affordability), and drought/post-war supply hour restrictions in 1945–1953 (service_continuity).
outcome_flags.value: formal_connection, water_access, sanitation_access, service_coverage, service_quantity, service_quality, affordability, service_continuity

sample_size.comment: Single-city historical-institutional case study of Barcelona (1867–1967) using archival documents (AMCB, AHCB, Fundacion AGBAR Fonds) and aggregate historical water supply/consumption series (1910–1945 and 1950–1974); no household, individual, or multi-unit sample size is reported.

study_design.comment: 100-year historical-institutional case study tracing the infrastructural, legal-regulatory, corporate, and domestic transition of Barcelona's water supply and sanitation system using municipal and corporate archival sources and descriptive historical time series.
study_design.value: Historical-institutional case study (archival document analysis and descriptive historical statistics, 1867–1967)
study_design.where_found: PDF p. 2, Abstract; PDF pp. 4–20, archival citations and Figures 1–2

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 6, Section 'The Eixample district: from a public water supply to private undertakings'
evidence_quotes.quote: The passivity of local authorities favoured the appearance of private enterprises devoted to supplying the Eixample with water.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 8, Section 'The sanitation problem and the necessary increase in water consumption'
evidence_quotes.quote: Although 90 per cent of the streets had sewers, only 57 per cent of these were in good condition.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 16, Section 'Water’s slow entry into the domestic sphere'
evidence_quotes.quote: Generally speaking, the attempts to improve facilities and to increase consumption for health reasons ran up against the resistance of tenement house owners, because it was not easy to pass on the cost of improvements to poor working-class people. The economic straits of the times also prevented the spread of water meters, as opposed to what was provided in the Municipal Health Regulations approved by Royal Decree in 1925.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 16, Section 'Water’s slow entry into the domestic sphere'
evidence_quotes.quote: Some urban areas were clearly excluded from the new services, above all in the peripheral working-class districts that arose in the 1920s and 1930s, where there was a very low level of urban development and very limited access to technical networks.

evidence_quotes.page: PDF Page 18, Section 'From post-war restrictions to widespread water consumption'
evidence_quotes.quote: The water from the Ter River arrived in 1966 in a token amount but in 1967 this supply became substantial, exceeding that of the Llobregat River.
Barcelona City Council tried to update and expand the municipal water supply and in the early twentieth century it sought to municipalize the SGAB, but both these initiatives were complete failures.
